# Overview

## What This Talk Covers

\begin{columns}
\begin{column}{0.55\textwidth}

\textbf{Research Question}

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=ensaiblue!8, colframe=ensaiblue, arc=4pt, boxrule=0.8pt]
Which spatial interpolation algorithm is most effective when \textbf{only coordinates} are available as predictors?
\end{tcolorbox}

\vspace{0.5em}
\textbf{Three algorithm families compared:}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \detbadge\ — IDW, K-NN
  \item \geobadge\ — Ordinary Kriging
  \item \mlbadge\ — RF, XGBoost, GAM, GeoRF, \ldots
\end{itemize}

\vspace{0.5em}
\textbf{Key innovation tested:} Coordinate Rotation preprocessing for tree-based models

\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.42\textwidth}

\textbf{Evaluation dimensions}
\begin{itemize}
  \item[$\bullet$] \textbf{Accuracy} — R², RMSE, MAE
  \item[$\bullet$] \textbf{Scalability} — training time across dataset sizes
  \item[$\bullet$] \textbf{Robustness} — performance under noise
\end{itemize}

\vspace{0.8em}
\textbf{Talk roadmap}
\begin{enumerate}
  \item Problem \& datasets
  \item Algorithm families
  \item Results \& discussion
\end{enumerate}

\end{column}
\end{columns}


# Problem \& Data

## Spatial Interpolation — The Problem

\begin{columns}
\begin{column}{0.60\textwidth}

\textbf{Definition.} Given a set of observations $\{(s_i, z(s_i))\}_{i=1}^n$ at known locations $s_i \in \mathbb{R}^2$, estimate the value $z(s_0)$ at an \emph{unobserved} location $s_0$.

\vspace{0.6em}
\formulabox{ensaiblue}{
\textbf{Our setting}: predictors are \textbf{coordinates only} — no auxiliary covariates.\\
\vspace{0.2em}
This isolates the pure \textit{spatial} component of each algorithm.
}

\vspace{0.6em}
\textbf{Why it matters:}
\begin{itemize}
  \item Environmental monitoring, elevation modelling
  \item Climate interpolation, pollution mapping
  \item Large-scale IGN topographic data (France)
\end{itemize}

\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.37\textwidth}

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=detcol!10, colframe=detcol!60, arc=4pt, title={\textcolor{detcol}{\textbf{Challenge}}}]
Real spatial phenomena exhibit:
\begin{itemize}
  \item Spatial autocorrelation
  \item Anisotropy
  \item Large-scale trends
  \item Non-stationarity
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}

\vspace{0.4em}
\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=mlcol!10, colframe=mlcol!60, arc=4pt, title={\textcolor{mlcol}{\textbf{Open Question}}}]
Can ML methods match or surpass classical geostatistics when given only $(x, y)$?
\end{tcolorbox}

\end{column}
\end{columns}

## Evaluation Protocol

\begin{columns}
\begin{column}{0.52\textwidth}

\textbf{Metrics (held-out test set, 50\%)}

\vspace{0.3em}
\begin{tabular}{ll}
\toprule
\textbf{Metric} & \textbf{Measures} \\
\midrule
$R^2$ & Proportion of variance explained \\
RMSE & Error in original units (penalises outliers) \\
MAE  & Robust average error \\
Time & Wall-clock training time (seconds) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}

\vspace{0.6em}
\textbf{Validation:} Randomised Search + K-Fold CV
\begin{itemize}
  \item Small data: 20 iterations, 5-fold, 10-min timeout
  \item Large data: 5 iterations, 3-fold
\end{itemize}

\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.45\textwidth}

\textbf{Two-phase selection}

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=ensaiblue!8, colframe=ensaiblue, arc=4pt]
\textbf{Phase 1} — Screen all algorithms on small datasets ($N \leq 5{,}000$)\\[4pt]
$\Downarrow$\\[4pt]
Discard computationally infeasible methods\\[4pt]
$\Downarrow$\\[4pt]
\textbf{Phase 2} — Evaluate survivors on large, very large, and noisy data
\end{tcolorbox}

\vspace{0.4em}
\small Fixed seed \texttt{42} throughout — SSPCloud, Python 3.13, \texttt{n\_jobs=-1}

\end{column}
\end{columns}


# Algorithm Families

## Three Families at a Glance

\begin{columns}
\begin{column}{0.32\textwidth}
\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=detcol!12, colframe=detcol, arc=5pt, title={\textcolor{detcol}{\textbf{[1] Deterministic}}}]
\textbf{IDW \& K-NN}

\vspace{0.3em}
Fixed mathematical rules on spatial distances.\\[4pt]
\textbf{No training phase.}\\[4pt]
Highly interpretable, near-instantaneous.\\[4pt]
Implicit assumptions via hyperparameters ($p$, $k$).
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.32\textwidth}
\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=geocol!12, colframe=geocol, arc=5pt, title={\textcolor{geocol}{\textbf{[2] Geostatistical}}}]
\textbf{Ordinary Kriging}

\vspace{0.3em}
Models spatial data as a stochastic process.\\[4pt]
Learns spatial autocorrelation via variogram.\\[4pt]
\textbf{BLUP} — theoretically optimal.\\[4pt]
$O(n^3)$ complexity — scalability ceiling.
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.32\textwidth}
\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=mlcol!12, colframe=mlcol, arc=5pt, title={\textcolor{mlcol}{\textbf{[3] Machine Learning}}}]
\textbf{RF, XGBoost, GAM, GeoRF}

\vspace{0.3em}
Data-driven, optimise a loss function.\\[4pt]
No explicit spatial model.\\[4pt]
\textbf{Highly flexible \& scalable.}\\[4pt]
Spatial adaptation needed (axis-aligned splits).
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{column}
\end{columns}

\vspace{0.5em}
\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=accentgold!15, colframe=accentgold!80, arc=4pt, boxrule=0.8pt]
\centering
\textbf{Central hypothesis:} Coordinate Rotation can bridge the gap between ML methods and classical geostatistics — without modifying the algorithms themselves.
\end{tcolorbox}


## Deterministic Methods — IDW

\begin{columns}
\begin{column}{0.55\textwidth}

\detbadge\ \textbf{Inverse Distance Weighting}

\vspace{0.5em}
Prediction at $s_0$ is a distance-weighted average of observations:

\formulabox{detcol}{
$$\hat{z}(s_0) = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n w_i(s_0)\, z(s_i)}{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n w_i(s_0)}, \quad w_i(s_0) = \frac{1}{d(s_0, s_i)^p}$$
}

\vspace{0.4em}
\textbf{Key hyperparameter:} $p > 0$ (distance-decay exponent)
\begin{itemize}
  \item Large $p$ $\Rightarrow$ strong locality, nearby points dominate
  \item Small $p$ $\Rightarrow$ smoother surface, distant points contribute
\end{itemize}

\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.42\textwidth}

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=detcol!8, colframe=detcol!60, arc=4pt, title={\textcolor{detcol}{\textbf{Properties}}}]
\textbf{Advantages}
\begin{itemize}
  \item No training phase required
  \item Exact interpolation at observed locations
  \item Fully interpretable
\end{itemize}
\vspace{0.3em}
\textbf{Limitations}
\begin{itemize}
  \item Monotonic distance assumption
  \item Cannot model directional effects
  \item No uncertainty estimates
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}

\end{column}
\end{columns}


## Deterministic Methods — K-NN

\begin{columns}
\begin{column}{0.55\textwidth}

\detbadge\ \textbf{K-Nearest Neighbours}

\vspace{0.5em}
Prediction is the average of the $k$ closest observed values:

\formulabox{detcol}{
$$\hat{z}(s_0) = \frac{1}{k} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{N}_k(s_0)} z(s_i)$$
where $\mathcal{N}_k(s_0)$ is the set of $k$ nearest neighbours of $s_0$.
}

\vspace{0.4em}
\textbf{Key hyperparameter:} $k$ (bandwidth)
\begin{itemize}
  \item Small $k$ $\Rightarrow$ highly local, noisy predictions
  \item Large $k$ $\Rightarrow$ strong smoothing, slowly-varying surface
\end{itemize}

\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.42\textwidth}

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=detcol!8, colframe=detcol!60, arc=4pt, title={\textcolor{detcol}{\textbf{Comparison with IDW}}}]
\vspace{0.2em}
Both rely on \textbf{geometric principles only} — no underlying statistical model.

\vspace{0.4em}
K-NN uses a \textbf{hard neighbourhood} (top-$k$), while IDW uses a \textbf{soft weighted average} of all points.

\vspace{0.4em}
Both serve as a \textbf{demanding baseline}: any ML method must justify its added complexity.
\end{tcolorbox}

\end{column}
\end{columns}


## Geostatistical Method — Ordinary Kriging

\begin{columns}
\begin{column}{0.55\textwidth}

\geobadge\ \textbf{Ordinary Kriging (OK)}

\vspace{0.4em}
Treats $z(s)$ as a realisation of a \textbf{stochastic process}.

\formulabox{geocol}{
$$\hat{Z}(s_0) = \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i\, Z(s_i), \quad \text{s.t.} \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i = 1$$
Weights $\lambda_i$ minimise $\mathrm{Var}\!\left(\hat{Z}(s_0) - Z(s_0)\right)$
}

\vspace{0.3em}
Weights are obtained via the \textbf{variogram} $\gamma(h)$, which describes how spatial similarity decays with distance $h$.

\vspace{0.3em}
\textbf{Result:} OK is the \textbf{BLUP} (Best Linear Unbiased Predictor) under its assumptions.

\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.42\textwidth}

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=geocol!8, colframe=geocol!60, arc=4pt, title={\textcolor{geocol}{\textbf{Strengths}}}]
\begin{itemize}
  \item Exact interpolation at data points
  \item Provides prediction uncertainty
  \item Explicitly models autocorrelation
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}

\vspace{0.3em}
\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=mlcol!10, colframe=mlcol!60, arc=4pt, title={\textcolor{mlcol}{\textbf{Critical Limitations}}}]
\begin{itemize}
  \item $O(n^3)$: infeasible for $n \gg 10{,}000$
  \item Assumes \textbf{stationarity} \& \textbf{isotropy}
  \item Variogram fitting is partly subjective
  \item Linear — struggles with nonlinear patterns
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}

\end{column}
\end{columns}


## Geostatistical Method — The Variogram

\begin{columns}
\begin{column}{0.52\textwidth}

The variogram $\gamma(h)$ is the core of Kriging:

\formulabox{geocol}{
$$\gamma(h) = \frac{1}{2} \mathrm{Var}\!\left(Z(s+h) - Z(s)\right)$$
}

\vspace{0.4em}
\textbf{Key parameters to estimate:}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Nugget}: discontinuity at origin (measurement error)
  \item \textbf{Sill}: total variance ($\gamma \to \text{sill}$ as $h \to \infty$)
  \item \textbf{Range}: distance at which correlation vanishes
\end{itemize}

\vspace{0.4em}
\textbf{Model selection}: spherical, exponential, Gaussian, Matérn — partly subjective, sensitive to outliers.

\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.45\textwidth}

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=geocol!8, colframe=geocol!50, arc=4pt, title={\textcolor{geocol}{\textbf{Stationarity Assumption}}}]
OK requires \textbf{intrinsic stationarity}:
\begin{itemize}
  \item Constant mean over the domain
  \item $\gamma(h)$ depends only on lag distance, not absolute location
\end{itemize}
\vspace{0.3em}
\small Often violated in practice: elevation varies between valleys and mountain ranges; temperature follows latitudinal gradients; housing prices radiate from urban centres.
\end{tcolorbox}

\end{column}
\end{columns}


## Machine Learning Methods — Overview

\begin{columns}
\begin{column}{0.48\textwidth}

\mlbadge\ \textbf{Paradigm shift}

\vspace{0.3em}
ML methods are \textbf{data-driven}: they learn predictive mappings $f(x,y) \to z$ by optimising a loss function, without any explicit spatial model.

\vspace{0.4em}
\textbf{Two sub-families in this benchmark:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=mlcol!8, colframe=mlcol!60, arc=4pt]
\textbf{1. Tree-based Ensembles}\\
Random Forest, XGBoost, GeoRF, Oblique RF, MI-GBT

\vspace{0.3em}
\textbf{2. Generalized Additive Models}\\
GAM — smooth nonlinear functions of coordinates
\end{tcolorbox}

\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.48\textwidth}

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=ensaiblue!8, colframe=ensaiblue, arc=4pt, title={\textbf{Key Advantages vs Classical Methods}}]
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{No distributional assumptions} — no stationarity, no isotropy required
  \item \textbf{Scalable} — can handle millions of points
  \item \textbf{Extensible} — covariates (land use, slope, \ldots) can be added seamlessly
  \item \textbf{Flexible} — model complex nonlinear surfaces
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}

\vspace{0.3em}
\textbf{Key challenge:} standard tree-based models use \textbf{axis-aligned splits} — ill-suited to oblique spatial gradients.

\end{column}
\end{columns}


## Tree-Based Methods — Random Forest

\begin{columns}
\begin{column}{0.52\textwidth}

\textbf{Random Forest (Bagging strategy)}

\vspace{0.3em}
Multiple decision trees trained on \textbf{bootstrap samples}; predictions are \textbf{averaged}:
$$\hat{z}(s_0) = \frac{1}{B} \sum_{b=1}^B T_b(s_0)$$

Each tree partitions the feature space via \textbf{recursive binary splits} minimising prediction error.

\vspace{0.4em}
Aggregation of \textbf{decorrelated trees} $\Rightarrow$ reduced variance, stable predictions.

\vspace{0.4em}
\textbf{Parameters:} \texttt{n\_estimators=50}, \texttt{max\_features=sqrt}, \texttt{min\_samples\_leaf=10}

\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.45\textwidth}

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=mlcol!8, colframe=mlcol!60, arc=4pt, title={\textcolor{mlcol}{\textbf{Spatial Challenge}}}]
Decision trees split along a \textbf{single coordinate axis} at each node.

\vspace{0.3em}
A diagonal spatial gradient (NW→SE elevation increase) requires many horizontal + vertical steps to approximate.

\vspace{0.3em}
$\Rightarrow$ Deep trees, high variance, inefficient representation.
\end{tcolorbox}

\vspace{0.3em}
\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=detcol!10, colframe=detcol!50, arc=3pt, boxrule=0.6pt]
\small In our benchmark: \textbf{RF} vs \textbf{RF + Coordinate Rotation} directly tests how much axis-alignment hurts.
\end{tcolorbox}

\end{column}
\end{columns}


## Tree-Based Methods — Gradient Boosting & XGBoost

\begin{columns}
\begin{column}{0.52\textwidth}

\textbf{Gradient Boosting (Sequential strategy)}

\vspace{0.3em}
Trees built \textbf{sequentially}: each new tree corrects the residuals of the current ensemble:
$$F_m(s) = F_{m-1}(s) + \eta \cdot T_m(s)$$

\vspace{0.3em}
\textbf{XGBoost}: state-of-the-art GB implementation with second-order gradient approximation, regularisation ($L_1$, $L_2$), and histogram binning.

\vspace{0.4em}
\textbf{Parameters:} \texttt{n\_estimators=200}, \texttt{max\_depth=15}, \texttt{learning\_rate=0.3}, \texttt{max\_bin=2000}

\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.45\textwidth}

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=mlcol!8, colframe=mlcol!60, arc=4pt, title={\textcolor{mlcol}{\textbf{RF vs XGBoost}}}]
\begin{tabular}{lll}
 & \textbf{RF} & \textbf{XGB} \\
\midrule
Strategy & Bagging & Boosting \\
Trees & Parallel & Sequential \\
Bias/Var & Low bias & Lower bias \\
Tuning & Robust & Sensitive \\
Overfit & Low risk & Moderate \\
\end{tabular}
\end{tcolorbox}

\vspace{0.3em}
\textbf{MI-GBT}: gradient boosting with a spatial loss function — explicitly penalises spatially correlated errors.

\end{column}
\end{columns}


## ML Methods — GeoRF \& Oblique RF

\begin{columns}
\begin{column}{0.48\textwidth}

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=mlcol!10, colframe=mlcol, arc=5pt, title={\textcolor{mlcol}{\textbf{Geographic Random Forest}}}]
Extends RF by incorporating \textbf{spatial structure} directly into ensemble construction.

\vspace{0.3em}
Trees are built on \textbf{geographically weighted} subsamples, making local predictions more sensitive to nearby observations.

\vspace{0.3em}
\textbf{Trade-off}: captures spatial heterogeneity, but \textbf{very high training cost} — found infeasible on large datasets in Phase 1.
\end{tcolorbox}

\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.48\textwidth}

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=geocol!10, colframe=geocol, arc=5pt, title={\textcolor{geocol}{\textbf{Oblique Random Forest}}}]
Removes the axis-alignment constraint: splits are \textbf{linear combinations of features}:
$$a_1 x + a_2 y \leq \theta$$

\vspace{0.2em}
Directly learns the best oblique boundary at each node.

\vspace{0.3em}
\textbf{Trade-off}: more expressive splits, but \textbf{computationally demanding} — each node optimisation is harder.
\end{tcolorbox}

\end{column}
\end{columns}

\vspace{0.4em}
\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=accentgold!15, colframe=accentgold!80, arc=4pt]
\centering
Both strategies address the axis-alignment problem \textbf{by modifying the algorithm}. Our Coordinate Rotation approach addresses it \textbf{by transforming the data} — simpler, faster, and more portable.
\end{tcolorbox}


## ML Methods — Generalized Additive Models

\begin{columns}
\begin{column}{0.55\textwidth}

\mlbadge\ \textbf{GAM} — boundary between statistics and ML

\vspace{0.4em}
GAMs model the target as a \textbf{sum of smooth nonlinear functions}:

\formulabox{geocol}{
$$z(s) = \beta_0 + f_1(x) + f_2(y) + \varepsilon$$
where $f_1, f_2$ are estimated smooth splines.
}

\vspace{0.3em}
Extensions include \textbf{bivariate smooths} $f(x, y)$ (thin-plate splines), capturing 2D spatial surfaces.

\vspace{0.4em}
\textbf{GAM vs tree-based:}
\begin{itemize}
  \item More \textbf{interpretable} — each smooth can be plotted
  \item Less expressive for \textbf{complex interactions}
  \item Slower than RF/XGB on large data
\end{itemize}

\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.42\textwidth}

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=mlcol!10, colframe=mlcol!60, arc=4pt, title={\textcolor{mlcol}{\textbf{In our benchmark}}}]
GAM with coordinate rotation variant tested: \textbf{GAM-CR} adds rotated coordinates as additional smoothing terms.

\vspace{0.4em}
\textbf{Excluded from large-scale} analysis (Phase 2): training time was prohibitive even on $N = 5{,}000$ datasets — extrapolation to millions of points is infeasible.
\end{tcolorbox}

\vspace{0.4em}
\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=ensaiblue!8, colframe=ensaiblue, arc=3pt, boxrule=0.6pt]
\small GAM results serve as an important \textbf{interpretability reference} in the small-data regime.
\end{tcolorbox}

\end{column}
\end{columns}


## Summary — Algorithm Families

\begin{columns}
\begin{column}{0.32\textwidth}
\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=detcol!12, colframe=detcol, arc=5pt, title={\textcolor{detcol}{\textbf{Deterministic}}}]
\small
\textbf{IDW, K-NN}\\[4pt]
\textcolor{geocol}{$\checkmark$} Near-zero training time\\
\textcolor{geocol}{$\checkmark$} Exact interpolation\\
\textcolor{geocol}{$\checkmark$} Fully interpretable\\[4pt]
\textcolor{mlcol}{$\times$} No spatial structure learning\\
\textcolor{mlcol}{$\times$} Brittle under noise\\
\textcolor{mlcol}{$\times$} No uncertainty estimates
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.32\textwidth}
\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=geocol!12, colframe=geocol, arc=5pt, title={\textcolor{geocol}{\textbf{Geostatistical}}}]
\small
\textbf{Ordinary Kriging}\\[4pt]
\textcolor{geocol}{$\checkmark$} Theoretically optimal (BLUP)\\
\textcolor{geocol}{$\checkmark$} Uncertainty quantification\\
\textcolor{geocol}{$\checkmark$} Explicit autocorrelation\\[4pt]
\textcolor{mlcol}{$\times$} $O(n^3)$ — ceiling at $\sim$10k pts\\
\textcolor{mlcol}{$\times$} Stationarity \& isotropy assumed\\
\textcolor{mlcol}{$\times$} Variogram fitting subjective
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.32\textwidth}
